analysis.one_liner: Cuts estate tax rates by 20 percent and shields the first $3 million of an estate.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee when Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut every estate tax rate by 20 percent and raise the amount of an estate exempted from tax to $3 million, with that amount rising with inflation after 2005. Only estates above roughly $1.5 to $2 million owed any estate tax at the time, so the change would go almost entirely to the largest estates. The bill was introduced in April 2005 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. In 2005 an estate paid no tax below $1.5 million, so raising the shield to $3 million would erase tax entirely on estates between those levels, and the 20 percent rate cut would lower the bill for every taxable estate, with the biggest savings going to the biggest estates. Families below those levels were already exempt and would see no change.

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts each estate and gift tax rate in the rate schedule by 20 percent — for example, the top rate drops from 48 percent to 39.2 percent, and lower brackets fall proportionally.
It raises the unified credit to the equivalent of a $3 million exclusion, meaning an estate worth up to $3 million would owe no estate tax at all.
Starting in 2006, the $3 million exclusion would be adjusted upward each year for inflation, rounded to the nearest $10,000.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Estate tax revenue would fall by the value of the rate cut and the newly exempted $1.5-to-$3-million band, a loss that must be made up through other taxes, more borrowing, or lower spending — a cost spread across everyone, while the savings concentrate in a few thousand large estates a year.

drawbacks.text: The tax cut is concentrated: only estates above the existing exemption owe any estate tax, so the entire benefit goes to the heirs of the largest estates, while the lost revenue is a cost borne by all federal taxpayers.
Because the exclusion rises to $3 million and then grows with inflation indefinitely, the revenue cost compounds over time rather than staying fixed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it reaches only a few thousand very large estates each year, since smaller estates were already exempt. The cost is a permanent loss of federal revenue shared by everyone, with the largest savings flowing to the largest estates. An honest supporter would concede the bill does little for ordinary families and much for wealthy ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled it for a hearing or vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Nita Lowey introduced the Estate Tax Reduction Act of 2005 on April 13, 2005.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained an advantage from the bill itself; federal revenue was preserved because the estate tax cut was never enacted, a result that favored general taxpayers over the heirs of large estates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers, since the tax cut never happened

for.name: Rep. Nita Lowey
for.role: Sponsor, Estate Tax Reduction Act of 2005
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 13, 2005; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Bill Thomas)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on April 13, 2005 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors of either party and never reached a vote, so no partisan split shows up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have cut their estate tax bill by up to 20 percent and exempted estates up to $3 million; because it died, their taxes stayed as they were. Their gain would have come directly out of federal revenue that everyone else depends on.

A $3 million inflation-indexed shield would have spared many estates from tax planning altogether, cutting demand for estate-planning work, while lower rates on large estates kept some high-end planning business alive.
